title: Cascade decode attention over the shared prefix
mechanism: Market traffic sends ~20k input tokens per request, most of which is a shared prompt prefix (instrument definitions, system prompt, schema). Stock decode reads each running sequence's whole KV independently, so the KV-read term grows linearly with batch size and never amortises. Split the decode attention into two levels: run one batched attention over the single physical copy of the shared prefix KV with all B query vectors stacked (arithmetic intensity rises by a factor of B because that KV is read once for the whole batch), run per-sequence attention over the short unique suffix, then combine the two partial outputs with the log-sum-exp merge that already exists in-tree (merge_state). Stock SGLang only builds cascade wrappers for speculative target-verify with topk>1, never for ordinary multi-request decode, so the prefix KV is re-read once per sequence today. This converts the dominant non-amortising term into one that amortises with batch size, which is exactly the term the methodology found stuck at 22-28% of H100 bandwidth.
hypothesis: Two-level cascade decode attention over the radix-cache shared prefix will lower cost per output token because the shared prefix KV is read from HBM once per decode step instead of once per sequence, making the KV-read term amortise with batch size.
source_title: 5.3.1 Prefix Caching and KV Cache Re-Use
expected_gain: The book gives no number for cascade decode. First-principles: if a fraction f of the 22k-token context is shared across a decode batch of B, per-step KV bytes fall by roughly f*(1-1/B). For f=0.8 and B=16 that is a ~75% cut in KV bytes read, and the KV read is the dominant decode term at this context length.
risks: Numerically the merge is exact (log-sum-exp), so no accuracy risk if implemented correctly; the risk is a wrong LSE merge silently corrupting outputs. Requires all sequences in a batch to share a prefix, so gains collapse on diverse traffic. Adds a second kernel launch and CUDA-graph shape variants per (prefix length, batch) pair.
prerequisites: Radix cache must expose the longest common prefix across the current decode batch; batch composition should group requests by prefix (see the prefix-affinity batching record); LSE-returning decode kernels for both levels.

title: Sub-8-bit KV cache with fused Triton dequant on Hopper
mechanism: Decode cost per output token at 20k context is set by bytes of KV moved per step. The book puts KV cache at moderate quantisation sensitivity and names blockwise microscaling formats as the way to keep dynamic range while cutting bits. Store K and V at 4 bits with a per-32-or-16-element block scale factor held inline next to the block, and dequantise inside the decode attention kernel as the block is loaded into registers, so the low-precision bytes are the only thing that ever crosses HBM. Stock SGLang already has FP8 e4m3/e5m2 and an mxfp8 KV dtype, and it has an FP4 KV quant method, but the FP4 decode path is routed to TRT-LLM MHA kernels that need Blackwell; on an H100 there is no sub-8-bit KV decode path. Writing the dequant into the Triton decode kernel supplies that path and halves KV bytes again relative to FP8.
hypothesis: Storing the KV cache at 4 bits with per-block scale factors and dequantising inside the decode attention kernel will lower cost per output token because it halves the bytes read per decode step relative to FP8 without a separate dequant pass through memory.
expected_gain: The book states quantising down one level of precision generally gives 30 to 50 percent better performance for LLMs (p.122), and that decode 'loads half as much data per value, effectively doubling memory bandwidth'. FP8 to FP4 is one further level, so expect the KV-read term to roughly halve again minus scale-factor overhead (~6% extra bytes at block 16).
risks: The book warns KV cache errors compound token to token because each token's KV is used by every subsequent token, and that 4-bit formats lose dynamic range. Expect measurable GSM8K/perplexity regression unless block size is small and outlier channels are held back at higher precision. Dequant arithmetic inside the kernel can eat the bandwidth win if it spills registers.
prerequisites: A calibration pass to fit block scales; the quality gate (GSM8K) must run every sweep; Triton decode kernel must accept a packed dtype plus a scale tensor; CUDA-graph capture must handle the extra buffer.

title: Query-aware sparse KV page selection at decode
mechanism: Not every one of the 20k cached tokens matters to the token being generated. Keep per-page bounding-box statistics (per-dimension min and max of the keys in that page), use them to compute a cheap upper bound on the attention score each page could contribute to the current query, and read the full KV only for the top-k pages. The bounding-box tensors are two orders of magnitude smaller than the KV they summarise, so the per-step read becomes O(k*page_size) instead of O(20k). SGLang 0.5.18 ships a Quest implementation under mem_cache/sparsity, but it is not on by default and its backend adaptor only covers fa3/flashattention and the DeepSeek DSA path; wiring it for the dense-GQA decode path used here, and tuning k against the SLO, is the work.
hypothesis: Selecting the top-k KV pages per query with bounding-box score bounds and reading only those pages will lower cost per output token because per-step KV bytes drop by the sparsity ratio while attention output stays close enough to dense to hold GSM8K accuracy.
expected_gain: The book gives no figure for training-free sparse decode attention. Mechanically, reading k of P pages cuts the KV term to k/P plus the bounding-box read; at 20k tokens with 64-token pages and k chosen for 10-20% density this is a 5-10x reduction in KV bytes. Realised gain will be smaller because the bounding-box scan itself is a memory pass.
risks: Lossy: the book stresses attention is the most sensitive part of the model and that errors accumulate over thousands of autoregressive steps. Recall failures on long-range dependencies show up as wrong answers, not crashes. The score bound is an upper bound, so it over-selects on some heads and under-selects on others.
prerequisites: Bounding-box pools maintained on every KV write; a decode kernel that takes a per-request page index list; accuracy gate on a long-context eval, not just GSM8K.

title: Attention-sink plus sliding-window KV retention
mechanism: Turn the KV cache from something that grows to 22k entries per sequence into a fixed-size ring. Keep the first few tokens (the attention sink that soaks up excess softmax mass) plus the most recent w tokens, and free everything in between as soon as it falls out of the window. The book's argument is that tokens near each other in a sequence affect each other more than tokens from much earlier, and that sliding window attention turns O(N^2) into O(Nw). Applied at inference to a full-attention model this is training-free and bounds both the per-step KV read and the per-sequence footprint, which raises the batch size that fits in the 80GB H100 and so amortises the weight read as well. SGLang has SWA memory pools and SWA radix cache, but they are driven by the model config for models actually trained with SWA; applying a retention window to a full-attention checkpoint is a separate policy.
hypothesis: Retaining only attention-sink tokens plus a sliding window of recent KV will lower cost per output token because the per-step KV read and per-sequence memory footprint both become constant in context length instead of linear.
expected_gain: The book gives the complexity change (O(N^2) to O(Nw), with w commonly 8K to 32K) but no accuracy-preserving figure for retrofitting onto a non-SWA model. For a 20k prompt, w=4k would cut the KV term roughly 5x; whether accuracy survives is the whole question. Expected gain: unknown.
risks: The book is explicit that sliding window works well when applied during training. Dropping middle context from a full-attention model loses information the model was trained to use; for 20k-token market prompts the evicted middle is likely to hold the data the answer depends on. High chance of accuracy loss.
prerequisites: Retention policy plumbed through the allocator and radix cache so evicted blocks are actually freed; a long-context accuracy gate; per-layer window sizes if only some layers tolerate it.

title: Progressive KV compression of older context
mechanism: Instead of dropping old tokens outright, merge them. The book describes compressed attention as periodically compressing context from earlier in the sequence so that attention considers both compressed context and uncompressed recent tokens. Concretely: once a page ages past a threshold, replace its n token KV entries with m << n synthesised entries (for example a weighted merge of keys within a page and the corresponding value average, or a small learned pooling), keeping recent pages verbatim. The decode kernel then attends over compressed-plus-recent, so per-step KV bytes fall with context age rather than growing linearly. This differs from eviction because information from every token still contributes to the merged entry, which is why it should degrade more gracefully than a hard window.
hypothesis: Merging aged KV pages into a smaller number of summary entries will lower cost per output token because the per-step KV read grows sub-linearly with context length while retaining a lossy trace of every token.
expected_gain: The book names the technique but gives no numbers. Compression ratio is a free parameter; a 4:1 merge on everything older than the most recent 4k tokens cuts the 22k-token KV read to roughly 8.5k equivalent entries, a ~2.5x reduction. Expected gain: unknown without measurement.
risks: Lossy and irreversible; once merged, the original KV is gone and a later request that hits the same prefix in the radix cache inherits the compressed version. Merged keys are not real keys, so RoPE phase relationships and softmax scaling become approximate. Interacts badly with prefix caching correctness expectations.
prerequisites: A merge kernel run off the critical path; radix cache must mark compressed nodes so they are not treated as exact prefix matches; accuracy gate on long-context tasks.

title: Low-rank latent KV cache
mechanism: Multi-latent attention approximates attention in a low-dimensional latent space, storing one compact latent vector per token instead of separate K and V vectors for every KV head. Retrofit the idea onto the served checkpoint by factorising the per-layer K and V projection weights (SVD, or a short calibration fit), caching only the low-rank latent c_t of width r << H_kv*d, and folding the up-projection into the query side so the decode kernel computes scores directly against the latent. Bytes moved per token per layer drop from 2*H_kv*d to r. Because the up-projection is absorbed into Q, no extra HBM traffic is created. SGLang already has an MLA-shaped memory pool and MLA attention backends for DeepSeek-class models, so the pool and backend abstractions exist to target; what is missing is a path that turns a GQA checkpoint into a latent-KV one.
hypothesis: Caching a low-rank latent per token instead of full K and V, with the up-projection absorbed into the query, will lower cost per output token because per-token KV bytes fall by the compression ratio r/(2*H_kv*d) with no extra memory traffic added elsewhere.
expected_gain: The book describes MLA qualitatively and notes SGLang works with labs to implement it, but gives no ratio. Appendix B also lists tensor-decomposition KV compression as a research direction. Achievable rank depends on the spectrum of the trained K/V projections; expected gain: unknown until the singular values are measured.
risks: A trained-in architecture is being approximated post hoc, so reconstruction error hits attention, the most quantisation-sensitive part of the model per the book. The book also notes MLA as implemented in PyTorch is awkward to export and needs hand-fused kernels. Absorbing the up-projection into Q changes the shape of every attention kernel call.
prerequisites: SVD/calibration of K and V projections per layer; a latent KV pool; an MLA-style decode kernel that accepts the absorbed query; accuracy validation against the dense baseline.

title: GQA head-group packing in the decode kernel
mechanism: In grouped-query attention several query heads share one KV head. If the decode kernel assigns one CUDA block per query head, the same KV block is fetched from HBM once per query head in the group, multiplying the KV-read term by the group size and leaving achieved bandwidth low because the redundant fetches contend for the same lines. Restructure the decode kernel so a block loads a KV tile for one KV head into shared memory once and computes scores for all query heads in that group from the resident tile, turning a stack of GEMVs into a small GEMM that can use Tensor Cores. This is the within-sequence counterpart to the cascade idea's cross-request amortisation and is a pure kernel change with no numerical approximation, which is why it is worth trying before any lossy technique. The book frames exactly this as the FlashAttention lesson: same mathematical operation, restructured to eliminate excess reads and fit the GPU.
hypothesis: Packing all query heads that share a KV head into one kernel block so the KV tile is fetched once per group will lower cost per output token because it removes redundant HBM traffic and raises arithmetic intensity by the GQA group size, without changing the computed result.
expected_gain: The book gives no number, but the arithmetic-intensity argument in 2.4.1 is direct: intensity rises by the GQA ratio if the KV tile is reused across the group. For a typical ratio of 4-8 this is the difference between a GEMV and a small GEMM. Lossless, so any measured speedup is bankable.
risks: None numerically (bitwise-comparable up to reduction order). Practical risks are shared-memory pressure limiting the tile size, reduced occupancy from bigger blocks, and interaction with the existing KV-split heuristic which may already be splitting work in a way that conflicts.
prerequisites: Confirm the model's GQA group size from config; profile the current decode kernel with Nsight Compute to confirm redundant KV traffic is actually happening before rewriting.

title: KV layout repack for coalesced wide loads
mechanism: Achieved decode bandwidth of 22-28% is the signature of a read pattern that does not coalesce into full memory transactions. Paged KV is addressed through an indirection table, and if the innermost layout is [page, head, token, dim] each warp lane ends up striding across head or token boundaries, so a 128-byte transaction delivers only the fraction of bytes the warp actually wants. Repack the pool so the fastest-varying axis is head_dim and consecutive lanes read consecutive 16-byte vectors within one page-head tile, size pages so a tile is a whole number of 128-byte lines, and issue 128-bit vectorised loads. SGLang has a page-major layout module and a paged allocator, so the layout is already parameterised; the change is choosing and measuring the layout that saturates HBM for this model's head geometry.
hypothesis: Repacking the paged KV pool so decode reads are fully coalesced 128-bit vector loads within a page-head tile will lower cost per output token because the same logical bytes are delivered in fewer, fuller memory transactions, raising achieved bandwidth toward the 3.35 TB/s ceiling.
expected_gain: If the measured 22-28% of peak is transaction efficiency rather than latency, the headroom is the ratio itself: up to ~3x on the KV-read term before hitting other limits. The book supplies the ceiling (H100 at 3.35 TB/s) but no efficiency figure, so the size of the win is unknown until profiled.
risks: Lossless. Risks are mechanical: every kernel and backend that indexes the pool must be updated together, the hierarchical-cache host pool and the KV transfer paths assume a layout, and a wrong stride silently reads the wrong tokens rather than crashing.
prerequisites: Nsight Compute run on the decode attention kernel to record sectors-per-request and confirm coalescing is the problem; a layout abstraction all backends go through.

title: Hopper async pipelining and L2 residency for decode KV
mechanism: If the decode attention kernel loads KV synchronously, every SM stalls on HBM latency and bandwidth goes unused even with a perfect access pattern. The book notes Hopper introduced asynchronous data transfer and execution and that FlashAttention 3 exists precisely to exploit them. Restructure the decode kernel as a multi-stage software pipeline: issue bulk async copies (TMA / cp.async) for KV tile i+2 while computing on tile i, with enough stages in flight to cover HBM latency, and mark the shared prefix pages as L2-persistent so that the portion of KV reused across the batch stays in the 50MB L2 instead of returning to HBM every step. This attacks the achieved-bandwidth gap from the latency side, where layout repacking attacks it from the transaction-efficiency side.
hypothesis: Deep multi-stage async prefetch of KV tiles plus L2 persistence hints for shared pages will lower cost per output token because the decode kernel stops stalling on HBM latency and the hottest KV is served from L2 rather than HBM.
expected_gain: The book credits FlashAttention 3 with improved performance and memory efficiency on Hopper from exactly these features but gives no percentage. H100 L2 is 50MB (p.78), which at FP8 holds only a few hundred tokens of KV per layer, so the L2 half helps mainly for the shared-prefix cascade path. Expected gain: unknown.
risks: Lossless. Triton's control over TMA and L2 residency is limited, so this may require a custom CUDA kernel compiled with nvcc. Too many pipeline stages exhausts shared memory and cuts occupancy. L2 persistence set wrongly evicts weights and makes things slower.
prerequisites: nvcc in the image (available); Nsight Compute memory-workload analysis to distinguish latency-bound from bandwidth-bound before investing; CUDA-graph-compatible kernel launch.

title: Pre-RoPE key storage for position-independent KV reuse
mechanism: Keys are normally cached after rotary embedding is applied, which welds each cached key to the absolute position it had when it was written. That is why KV reuse only works for exact prefixes: the same text at a different offset has different cached keys. Store keys before RoPE and apply the rotation inside the decode and extend attention kernels using the position the token occupies in the current request. Cached KV then becomes position-independent, so a document chunk that appears at offset 3000 in one request and 7000 in another is a cache hit rather than a miss. For 20k-token market prompts assembled from recurring blocks in varying order this converts a large share of prefill into cache hits. The book identifies correcting positional embeddings as one of the two blockers to non-prefix KV reuse.
hypothesis: Caching keys pre-RoPE and applying rotation in-kernel at the current position will lower cost per output token because reusable context is no longer restricted to exact prefixes, raising cache hit rate and cutting prefill compute on 20k-token inputs.
source_title: 5.3.1 Prefix Caching and KV Cache Re-Use
expected_gain: The book gives no number; it only states that non-prefix reuse requires correcting positional embeddings and selectively recomputing KV entries. Gain scales with how much repeated-but-shifted content the real traffic contains, which is measurable from the trace database before implementing. Expected gain: unknown, traffic-dependent.
risks: Applying RoPE in-kernel adds arithmetic to the hottest kernel and needs the sin/cos tables resident, which can cost more bandwidth than it saves if done naively. Position-independent reuse is still an approximation: attention values for a chunk genuinely depend on what preceded it, so hit-rate gains can come with quality loss unless paired with selective recompute.
prerequisites: Measure repeated-block structure in the real trace first; kernels for both extend and decode must apply RoPE; radix cache keying must change from token-ids-with-position to token-ids alone.

title: Non-prefix KV reuse with selective recompute
mechanism: Prefix caching stops at the first token that differs, so a 20k-token prompt whose first token varies gets zero reuse even if the remaining 19,999 tokens are identical. The book names CacheBlend and LMCache as tools that support non-prefix sequences by correcting positional embeddings and selectively recomputing KV entries. Implement the recompute half: retrieve cached KV for matching chunks wherever they appear in the sequence, then recompute KV for only the small fraction of tokens whose attention is most perturbed by the changed context (selected by the largest deviation between cached and freshly computed keys on a probe layer), splicing the rest in unchanged. Prefill compute drops from O(N^2) over 20k tokens to O(N^2) over the recomputed subset.
hypothesis: Splicing cached KV for matching non-prefix chunks and recomputing only the most perturbed fraction of tokens will lower cost per output token because prefill FLOPs for 20k-token inputs fall roughly in proportion to the recomputed fraction while output quality stays within the accuracy gate.
source_title: 5.3.1 Prefix Caching and KV Cache Re-Use
expected_gain: The book cites the technique but no speedup. The CacheBlend line of work targets recomputing a small single-digit percentage of tokens; if that holds here, TTFT on cache-eligible 20k-token requests falls by close to an order of magnitude. Expected gain for cost per output token is smaller, since decode dominates a 2k-output request.
risks: Lossy in a way that is hard to bound: cross-chunk attention is genuinely different from what the spliced KV encodes. Needs the pre-RoPE storage change (or explicit position correction) to be sound at all. Chunk matching adds CPU work on the critical path for every request.
prerequisites: Position-independent key storage or an explicit RoPE-shift kernel; a chunk-level content-addressed index alongside the radix tree; a probe-layer heuristic for choosing recompute targets.

title: Per-layer KV precision allocation
mechanism: Uniform KV quantisation spends the same bits on layers with very different sensitivity. The book's video-model section gives the transferable rule directly: keep the first and last layers at high precision and quantise the hidden layers, because the outer layers take the input and produce the final output while hidden layers only perform intermediate calculations. Apply it to the KV cache: measure per-layer sensitivity once by quantising one layer at a time and scoring the eval, then allocate a bit budget so that insensitive middle layers hold 4-bit KV and sensitive outer layers hold FP8 or BF16. Because the cache is per-layer already, this is an allocation policy over the existing pool rather than a new format, and it buys most of the bandwidth reduction of aggressive quantisation at a fraction of the quality cost.
hypothesis: Allocating KV cache bit-width per layer according to measured per-layer sensitivity will lower cost per output token because total KV bytes fall close to the uniform-low-precision case while accuracy stays close to the uniform-high-precision case.
source_title: 6.6.1 Attention Optimization and Quantization (selective quantization by layer)
expected_gain: The book asserts the principle for video diffusion without numbers for LLMs. If two thirds of layers tolerate 4-bit and the rest stay at FP8, KV bytes fall about 33% versus all-FP8 with the accuracy profile of a much milder scheme. Expected gain: unknown until per-layer sensitivity is measured.
risks: Sensitivity measured on one eval may not transfer to production traffic. A mixed-width pool complicates allocation, eviction accounting and CUDA-graph shapes. The book's warning that KV errors compound token to token still applies to the quantised layers.
prerequisites: A per-layer sensitivity sweep harness; the pool must support heterogeneous per-layer dtypes; the sub-8-bit KV decode path from the fused-dequant record.

title: Layer-pipelined KV streaming from host memory
mechanism: The book lays out the KV storage hierarchy: device VRAM at terabytes per second, host RAM at tens to hundreds of gigabytes per second, then SSDs. SGLang's hierarchical cache already moves whole blocks between GPU and host between requests. The idea here is different and finer-grained: during a decode step, stream a given layer's cold KV from host memory over PCIe while the GPU is still computing the previous layers, so the transfer is hidden behind compute rather than serialised against it. That lets the resident GPU KV working set be smaller than the full context, freeing VRAM for a larger batch, which is the one thing that makes the weight-read term amortise. It only pays where PCIe bandwidth times the per-layer compute window exceeds the bytes needed, so it is a bet on overlap, not on raw bandwidth.
hypothesis: Prefetching each layer's cold KV from host memory one layer ahead of the compute front will lower cost per output token because it frees VRAM for a larger decode batch without adding stall time, amortising the weight read over more concurrent sequences.
source_title: 5.3.2 Where to Store the KV Cache
expected_gain: The book's table puts host memory at tens to hundreds of GB/s against terabytes per second on device, so on a PCIe H100 (not a Grace superchip, where the book notes NVLink-C2C gives up to 900 GB/s) the transfer budget per decode step is small. Likely only viable for a minority of cold layers. Expected gain: unknown and probably negative if the overlap does not hold.
risks: Straightforward way to make things much slower: any transfer that misses its overlap window stalls the whole decode step and blows the p90 TPOT budget. Adds PCIe contention with weight loading and output streaming. Complexity in the cache controller is high.
prerequisites: Pinned host buffers and a dedicated copy stream; measurement of actual PCIe bandwidth on the target instance; per-layer compute-time profile to size the prefetch window.

title: Shape-specialised decode kernel autotuning
mechanism: The book's point about kernel selection is that implementations are tied to exact hardware and shapes, and that picking the right kernel for a given matrix shape is itself an optimisation. The decode attention configuration space here is large (KV-split count, tile sizes on sequence and head_dim, number of warps, pipeline stages) and stock SGLang picks the split count from a fixed heuristic. Build a small offline autotuner that sweeps this space across the (batch, context length, head geometry) points the real traffic actually visits, records the best configuration per shape bucket in a cache keyed like the existing CUDA-graph shape keys, and has the backend look it up at dispatch. This is the cheapest way to attack a 22-28% bandwidth figure because it does not change any math and can be run overnight.
hypothesis: Autotuning decode attention tile and split configuration per (batch, context length) bucket instead of using a fixed heuristic will lower cost per output token because the default configuration is not optimal at the 20k-context, moderate-batch operating point this workload actually occupies.
expected_gain: No book figure. Triton autotuning on a mis-tuned memory-bound kernel commonly returns 1.2-1.6x; if the 22-28% figure is partly a tuning artefact the ceiling is higher. Lossless, low risk, so a good first experiment.
risks: Lossless numerically. Autotuning time is significant and must not run at request time; a stale cache after any kernel edit silently serves a bad configuration; CUDA graph capture must happen after the configuration is fixed.
prerequisites: The trace database to enumerate the real (batch, context) distribution; a benchmark harness that isolates the decode attention kernel; persistent autotune cache keyed by GPU and shape.

title: Persistent fused decode attention and output projection
mechanism: The book's kernel-fusion argument is that running two kernels back to back on the same data wastes a write and a read, and that during decode, the bandwidth-bound phase, an engine cannot afford unnecessary round trips. Today the decode attention kernel writes its per-head outputs to HBM, and the output projection GEMM reads them back, and then the residual add and the next RMSNorm each make another pass. Fuse attention, the output projection and the residual/norm into one persistent kernel that keeps the attention result in registers and shared memory across the whole block. The saved traffic is small next to the KV read itself, but it is entirely free of accuracy risk and it removes launch overhead and tail effects that hurt p90 TPOT at small batch.
hypothesis: Fusing decode attention with the output projection and the following residual-add and norm into one persistent kernel will lower cost per output token because the per-head attention output never round-trips through HBM and three kernel launches collapse into one.
source_title: 4.1.3 Reducing Memory Accesses with Kernel Fusion
expected_gain: The book gives the mechanism but no figure. The attention output for a decode step is tiny compared with the 20k-token KV read, so the bandwidth saving is a few percent at most; the launch-overhead and tail saving matters more at small batch. Expected gain: small but reliable, unknown magnitude.
risks: Lossless. A persistent kernel fixes the grid to the SM count, which can hurt when batch and head counts do not divide evenly. Fusing across the output projection means the GEMM can no longer use a tuned cuBLAS/DeepGEMM path, which may lose more than the fusion gains.
prerequisites: Profile first to confirm the projection and norm passes are visible in the decode step; CUDA-graph compatibility for the fused kernel.

title: Warp-specialised prefill and decode co-execution
mechanism: The book's case for disaggregation is that prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, and that specialising each is what unlocks performance; but disaggregation as described needs separate GPUs. On a single H100 the same asymmetry can be exploited in space rather than across machines: within one fused kernel, specialise warp groups so that some warps run the compute-bound prefill GEMM tiles on Tensor Cores while other warps run the memory-bound decode attention loads, using Hopper's asynchronous execution so the two occupy complementary hardware. Stock chunked prefill puts prefill and decode in the same batch but executes them as sequential kernels, so decode's idle Tensor Cores stay idle. Co-execution turns the memory-bound decode into free work hidden under prefill compute.
hypothesis: Co-executing prefill GEMM tiles and decode attention in warp-specialised groups within one kernel will lower cost per output token because decode's unused Tensor Core capacity is filled with prefill work instead of idling while the KV read completes.
expected_gain: The book gives no figure for single-GPU co-execution; its disaggregation numbers are about multi-GPU specialisation. Upper bound is the decode step's idle Tensor Core time, which at 22-28% memory utilisation and low arithmetic intensity is most of it. Expected gain: unknown, and gated on whether warp specialisation actually overlaps rather than serialising on shared memory.
risks: Hard to implement and easy to make slower through shared-memory and register contention. Mixing phases in one kernel makes p90 TTFT and p90 TPOT interact in ways that are hard to reason about; a long prefill tile can stall decode past the 25ms TPOT budget. Likely needs hand-written CUDA.
prerequisites: nvcc-compiled custom kernel; a scheduler that presents a mixed prefill/decode batch with known tile counts; careful SLO instrumentation to catch tail regressions.

title: Two-batch overlap of attention and MLP within one GPU
mechanism: Split the running batch into two micro-batches and software-pipeline them so that micro-batch A's memory-bound attention (the 20k-token KV read) executes concurrently with micro-batch B's compute-bound MLP GEMMs, then swap. Because the two phases bottleneck on different resources, running them together approaches the max of the two times rather than the sum. SGLang has a two-batch-overlap backend, but it exists to hide inter-GPU communication in multi-GPU MoE deployments; on a single H100 with no communication to hide, the same machinery can instead be pointed at the attention/MLP resource asymmetry the book describes in the roofline section. This is a scheduling-and-streams change rather than a new kernel, so it is much cheaper to try than warp specialisation.
hypothesis: Splitting the decode batch into two micro-batches and overlapping one's attention with the other's MLP will lower cost per output token because the memory-bound and compute-bound halves of the forward pass stop serialising.
expected_gain: The book supplies the roofline framing (H100 ops:byte 295 versus decode arithmetic intensity around 62, p.68) but no overlap figure. Ceiling is the smaller of the two phase times; realistically a fraction of that after synchronisation overhead. Expected gain: unknown.
risks: Halving the effective batch per micro-batch halves the weight-read amortisation, which can cancel the overlap win outright. Two in-flight micro-batches double activation memory. CUDA graph capture for two interleaved streams is fiddly and the scheduler must keep both micro-batches full or the pipeline drains.
prerequisites: Enough concurrency in the workload to fill two micro-batches; stream-aware CUDA graph capture; a per-phase timing breakdown to confirm attention and MLP times are comparable.

title: EAGLE-style speculative decoding to amortise the KV read
mechanism: Every decode forward pass pays the full 20k-token KV read to produce one token. Speculative decoding pays that read once and returns N+1 tokens: the draft head proposes N tokens, the target model verifies them all in a single pass over the same KV, and accepted tokens all come out of that one read. For a workload whose cost is dominated by a per-sequence KV read that does not amortise with batch size, speculation is the one lever that amortises it along the sequence axis instead. EAGLE is the book's recommended algorithm: a sub-billion-parameter draft model that consumes the target's hidden states from an early, middle and late layer rather than only the token, which is what gives it a high acceptance rate, and it can be attached to the same module as the target so there is no CPU round trip between draft and verify.
hypothesis: Attaching EAGLE draft heads and verifying N draft tokens per forward pass will lower cost per output token because the 20k-token KV read is paid once per accepted group of tokens instead of once per token.
expected_gain: The book says EAGLE generates sequences of up to eight draft tokens with a very high acceptance rate, roughly double Medusa's, and that the uplift is N+1 tokens per forward pass where N is the number accepted. Even a conservative 2-3 accepted tokens per pass divides the dominant KV-read term by the same factor.
risks: The book warns speculation is most useful at low batch sizes with spare compute and must be dynamically disabled at high batch sizes where compute is saturated; and that adopting EAGLE for latency requires reduced batch sizes, lowering throughput. Acceptance rate falls with temperature and varies by subject matter. Draft weights and their KV consume VRAM that would otherwise hold target KV.
prerequisites: Trained EAGLE heads for this checkpoint (train or distil them; none ship with the model); the target model must expose early/middle/late hidden states; tree-verify attention masks and CUDA graphs for the draft path.

title: Prompt-derived n-gram speculation
mechanism: With 20k input tokens and 2k output tokens, a large share of the output is likely to quote, restate or transform spans that already appear in the input. N-gram speculation exploits that without any draft model: while building the KV cache during prefill, also build a dictionary mapping each observed token to the sequence that followed it in the prompt; during decode, look the just-generated token up and offer the stored suffix as draft tokens for the target to verify in one pass. Draft generation costs a hash lookup rather than a forward pass, and the book notes n-gram sequences can exceed ten tokens where EAGLE manages about eight, so a single hit can amortise the 20k-token KV read over ten or more output tokens. Unlike EAGLE it needs no training, which makes it the cheapest speculation experiment to run first.
hypothesis: Building an n-gram dictionary from the 20k-token prompt during prefill and using it to propose draft tokens will lower cost per output token because output spans that echo the input are produced many-per-forward-pass at negligible draft cost.
expected_gain: The book states n-gram sequences can exceed ten tokens versus about eight for EAGLE, but that acceptance is only high when the output resembles the input, and that it is mostly used for code completion and revision where it easily outperforms EAGLE. Whether market-report traffic has that property is measurable from the trace database. Expected gain: unknown, entirely dependent on input/output overlap.
risks: Acceptance collapses when the output does not echo the input, and rejected drafts waste verification compute, so this can be a net loss on the wrong traffic. Once one draft token is rejected the whole remaining sequence is discarded. Same high-batch-size caveat as all speculation.
prerequisites: Measure input/output n-gram overlap on the real trace before enabling; dictionary construction must run off the critical path during prefill; verification masks and CUDA graphs for variable draft lengths.

title: 4-bit weight quantisation to buy KV headroom
mechanism: The 27B model at FP8 occupies roughly 27GB of the H100's 80GB, leaving the rest for KV. Requantising the linear layers to 4 bits with per-group scales (AWQ or GPTQ style, both in Appendix B's reading list) while keeping FP8 activations and compute roughly halves the weight footprint, which does two things at once: it halves the per-step weight-read term, and it frees on the order of 13GB for KV cache, which raises the batch size that fits at 20k context. A larger batch is the only mechanism that makes the weight read amortise, so the second effect compounds with the first. The book identifies linear-layer weights as the component least sensitive to quantisation, which is what makes this the safest place to spend precision.
hypothesis: Quantising linear-layer weights to 4 bits with group-wise scales while keeping FP8 activations will lower cost per output token because the weight-read term halves and the freed VRAM raises the feasible decode batch size at 20k context.
expected_gain: The book's rule of thumb is 30 to 50 percent better performance per level of precision halving, and it notes weights are the least sensitive component. Against the KV-dominated decode at 20k context the direct weight-read saving is secondary; the batch-size headroom from ~13GB freed is the larger effect and is bounded by how many extra 20k-context sequences that holds.
risks: The book cautions that integer formats lack dynamic range and are not suitable for quality-sensitive production workloads, and that early and late layers may need to stay at original precision. W4A8 dequant-to-FP8 on the fly adds compute to every GEMM and can slow prefill, which is compute-bound and sets TTFT. Marlin-style kernels are tuned for specific shapes and may not cover this model's.
prerequisites: An AWQ/GPTQ calibration run on representative market prompts; a W4A8 GEMM kernel that is actually faster than FP8 at these shapes; the GSM8K gate plus a perplexity check as the book recommends.

title: Activation outlier migration for lower-precision activations
mechanism: Activations sit second on the book's sensitivity ladder, above weights and below KV cache, and the thing that makes them hard to quantise is a small number of channels with very large magnitude that force a wide scale on every other channel. SmoothQuant, in Appendix B's reading list, migrates that difficulty offline: divide each activation channel by a per-channel factor and multiply the corresponding weight column by the same factor, which leaves the product unchanged but flattens the activation distribution so a narrow scale covers it. Applied here it makes the prefill GEMMs, which set TTFT and are compute-bound, safely runnable at lower precision, and it is a prerequisite for getting real gains out of any sub-FP8 activation path.
hypothesis: Migrating activation outliers into the weights with per-channel smoothing factors will lower cost per output token because it lets the prefill and decode GEMMs run at lower activation precision, doubling usable Tensor Core throughput, without the accuracy loss that naive activation quantisation causes.
expected_gain: The book gives 30 to 50 percent per precision level for LLMs generally and notes FP8 Tensor Cores are twice as fast as FP16. The model is already FP8, so the gain here is whatever a further step buys on the compute-bound prefill path; on H100 there is no FP4 Tensor Core, so this mainly protects quality rather than adding speed. Expected gain: small on H100, unknown.
risks: The smoothing factors are folded into weights offline, so a bad calibration set silently degrades every request. The book notes activation functions themselves are rarely quantised and softmax should stay at original precision. Benefit on Hopper is limited because there is no sub-FP8 Tensor Core path.
prerequisites: Calibration activations from real traffic; a weight-rewrite step at load time; verification that the fused FP8 GEMM path accepts the rescaled weights.

title: Block-sparse prefill attention for long prompts
mechanism: Prefill over a 20k-token prompt is compute-bound and quadratic in sequence length, and it sets TTFT against a 2818ms p90 budget. Attention maps at this length are strongly structured: most mass sits near the diagonal and on a few vertical strips (sink tokens, section headers). Compute prefill attention block-sparsely, evaluating only query-key block pairs selected by a cheap pooled-score pass (pool keys and queries per block, score the pooled pairs, keep the top blocks plus the diagonal and the sink column), and skip the rest. Attention FLOPs drop from O(N^2) toward O(N*w). This targets a different bottleneck from the decode-side sparsity records: prefill is compute-limited, not bandwidth-limited, so the win comes from skipped Tensor Core work rather than skipped memory traffic.
hypothesis: Computing prefill attention only over the top-scoring query-key block pairs plus diagonal and sink blocks will lower cost per output token because prefill FLOPs on 20k-token prompts fall roughly with the block density, freeing GPU time for decode within the same TTFT budget.
expected_gain: The book gives the complexity change for sliding-window attention, O(N^2) to O(Nw), but no measured accuracy-preserving density for training-free block sparsity. At 20k tokens with 10-20% block density the attention portion of prefill drops 5-10x; attention is only part of prefill, so end-to-end TTFT gain is smaller.
risks: Lossy, and the book warns that new attention algorithms trade quality for complexity and work best when applied during training. Missing a block that carried a long-range dependency corrupts the whole KV cache for that request, and the error then propagates through all 2k decode steps.
prerequisites: A pooled-score selection kernel cheap enough not to eat the saving; block-sparse FlashAttention kernel (NSA and MiniMax sparse scaffolding exists in-tree as reference); accuracy gate on long-context tasks.

title: Hybrid linear-attention layer substitution
mechanism: The most complete escape from the KV-read term is to stop having a KV cache in most layers. The book describes Mamba-style selective state-space models that replace self-attention with a recurrent state update achieving linear scaling on sequence length, and notes hybrid models mixing state-space blocks with transformer blocks are becoming more popular. Replace a fraction of this model's attention layers with gated linear-attention or state-space blocks whose per-sequence state is a fixed-size matrix independent of context length, keeping a minority of full-attention layers for exact recall, then recover quality by distilling from the original model. At 20k context the converted layers read a constant-size state instead of 20k tokens of KV, so the dominant term collapses on those layers. SGLang already carries hybrid linear-attention backends, Mamba kernels and hybrid KV pools, so the serving side exists; what does not exist is the converted checkpoint.
hypothesis: Converting a fraction of attention layers to gated-linear or state-space blocks with fixed-size recurrent state and distilling to recover quality will lower cost per output token because those layers' per-step state read is constant in context length instead of proportional to 20k tokens.
expected_gain: The book gives the complexity claim (linear scaling on sequence length) but explicitly says applications of state-space models are still limited. If half the layers convert, the KV-read term roughly halves and becomes context-independent on those layers. Expected gain: large in principle, unknown in practice, and unverifiable without training.
risks: This is the only record here that cannot be validated inside the serving stack alone: it needs a conversion and distillation run, and quality may not recover. Linear-attention layers are known to lose exact long-range retrieval, which matters for 20k-token prompts. Prefix caching semantics change because recurrent state is not sliceable the way KV is.
prerequisites: A conversion and distillation pipeline outside the serving loop; a hybrid checkpoint SGLang can load; hybrid cache pools configured for the mixed layer types; long-context retrieval evals.

title: Prefix-affinity decode batch composition
mechanism: Cache-aware routing sends requests that share a prefix to the same replica so they hit a warm cache. The same idea applied one level down, inside a single engine's scheduler, is batch composition: when choosing which waiting requests to admit into the running batch, prefer sets that share long radix-cache prefixes over sets that do not. Two payoffs. First, the shared prefix's KV is stored once instead of once per sequence, so more sequences fit in the same VRAM at 20k context. Second, it is the enabling condition for the cascade decode kernel, which can only amortise the KV read across a batch if the batch actually shares a prefix. Stock scheduling policies here order by length and priority and treat cache hits as a per-request TTFT benefit, not as a property of the batch as a whole.
hypothesis: Composing decode batches to maximise shared radix-cache prefix length will lower cost per output token because shared KV is stored and read once for the batch rather than once per sequence, raising both batch size and cascade attention effectiveness.
expected_gain: The book describes cache-aware routing across replicas without numbers and does not discuss intra-engine batch composition. The gain is whatever the cascade record's f (shared fraction) becomes once batches are chosen for it, so the two must be measured together. Expected gain: unknown alone, multiplicative with cascade attention.
risks: Reordering admission by prefix affinity starves requests with unpopular prefixes and can blow p90 TTFT, the exact metric under SLO. Needs a fairness bound or ageing term. Also risks convoying: a batch of identical prefixes finishes together and leaves the GPU idle.
prerequisites: Radix cache must answer 'longest common prefix among these candidate requests' cheaply; a fairness/ageing term in the policy; the cascade kernel to realise the second payoff.

title: SLO-driven closed-loop batch and chunk controller
mechanism: Batch size and prefill chunk size are set statically today, so they are tuned for an average that the traffic never actually is: too small when requests are short and the GPU is idle, too large when 20k-token prefills arrive together and p90 TPOT blows past 25ms. The book describes Dynamo's SLA-based planner operating on user-defined TTFT and TPS constraints and repeatedly frames batch sizing as the core latency-throughput lever. Build a controller inside the scheduler that measures p90 TTFT and p90/mean TPOT over a rolling window and adjusts running-batch size and prefill chunk size each step to sit at the largest batch that still meets the SLO. Because cost per output token falls monotonically with batch size until the SLO binds, running exactly at the SLO boundary rather than conservatively inside it is free throughput.
hypothesis: A controller that adjusts running batch size and prefill chunk size each step to hold measured p90 TTFT and p90 TPOT at their SLO limits will lower cost per output token because the engine runs at the largest SLO-feasible batch instead of a static conservative one.
expected_gain: No book figure. The gain is the gap between the static configuration's average utilisation and the SLO-feasible maximum, which the baseline sweep will reveal directly. If the current configuration is conservative, this is a large and entirely lossless win; if it is already at the boundary, it is nothing.
risks: A controller that chases p90 can oscillate or overshoot into sustained SLO violation; needs damping and a hard safety ceiling. p90 measured over a short window is noisy, and the book warns that outliers dominate percentile metrics. This is close in spirit to the knob-tweaking that has so far produced only noise, so it must be built as a controller, not a new constant.
prerequisites: Per-step latency instrumentation feeding the scheduler; a control law with hysteresis; the benchmark harness must report percentiles, not means.

title: Length-aware admission and preemption for p90 TTFT
mechanism: A 20k-token prefill occupies the GPU for many chunks, and any short request that arrives behind it waits for all of them. With a right-skewed latency distribution this head-of-line blocking is exactly what sets p90 TTFT, and the book stresses that good performance work focuses on reducing P90/P99 rather than the mean. Replace first-in-first-out admission with a length-aware discipline: estimate each queued request's prefill cost from its token count, and schedule so that a long prefill cannot monopolise more than a bounded share of consecutive steps, preempting and resuming it chunk-wise around shorter arrivals. Requests that are retracted keep their KV in the radix cache so resumption is cheap. SGLang has priority scheduling and retraction policies, but they act on an externally supplied priority integer rather than on a predicted service time.
hypothesis: Admitting and preempting requests by predicted prefill service time rather than arrival order will lower cost per output token because it removes head-of-line blocking from p90 TTFT, letting the engine run a larger batch at the same SLO instead of being sized for the worst case.
expected_gain: The book gives no figure, only the principle that P90/P99 matter more than the mean and that a request with 10,000 input tokens unbalances a system tuned for 100-token requests. With uniform 20k inputs the variance is low and this buys little; the gain scales with how heterogeneous the real ISL distribution turns out to be.
risks: Shortest-job-first style policies starve long requests, and market traffic's long requests may be the valuable ones. Preemption mid-prefill costs cache churn if the retracted KV gets evicted. Adds per-request estimation work to the scheduler hot loop.
prerequisites: ISL distribution from the trace database to confirm heterogeneity exists; retraction that preserves KV; an ageing term so long requests eventually run.

title: Online per-request policy selection across techniques
mechanism: The book warns that inference techniques are sometimes symbiotic and sometimes incompatible: quantising the KV cache relieves a disaggregation bottleneck, while increasing batch size removes the compute headroom speculation needs, and the engineer's job is a balanced set that delivers more than the sum of its parts. Every lossy or conditional technique in this bank has an operating region: speculation pays at low batch, sparsity pays at long context, cascade pays at high prefix sharing. Rather than picking one static configuration, add a policy layer that reads the current batch state (batch size, context lengths, measured prefix sharing, recent draft acceptance rate, headroom against the SLO) and turns each technique on or off per step. This is the meta-mechanism that makes the rest of the bank composable instead of mutually exclusive, and it is what turns per-technique wins that only hold in narrow regions into an aggregate win across real traffic.
hypothesis: Selecting speculation depth, KV sparsity level and cascade use per decode step from measured batch state will lower cost per output token because each technique is applied only in the operating region where it pays, instead of being statically on or off across all traffic.
expected_gain: No book figure. Value is conditional on at least two of the other records landing with different operating regions; on its own it does nothing. Expected gain: unknown, and strictly a second-order multiplier on the rest of the bank.
risks: Adds a combinatorial configuration space that is hard to attribute in benchmarks, and the book is explicit that only one variable should change at a time when benchmarking. A policy that switches techniques mid-request can produce inconsistent output quality within one response. Easy to build something unfalsifiable.
prerequisites: At least two other techniques implemented and independently measured with their operating regions mapped; per-step state already exposed to the scheduler; an attribution methodology that survives a dynamic policy.
